title: Protecting coasts: hard engineering or soft engineering?
examples: What is the difference between hard and soft engineering?

explain.say: Imagine your house is on a cliff, and every year the sea bites off almost 2 metres of your garden. On England’s Holderness coast that really happens. Look at the board: two ways to fight back, hard and soft.

draw.text: Protecting coasts: hard engineering or soft engineering?

explain.say: Look at the left: hard engineering, building strong things against the sea. A sea wall, like the one round Malé in the Maldives, throws waves back. Groynes are fences built across a beach to trap sand. Strong, but very expensive. Can you guess a problem?

Here is the catch. Groynes trap sand, so beaches further along get less sand and wear away faster. At Mappleton, on the Holderness coast, rock and groynes saved the village, but cliffs just to the south began eroding faster. Do you see how one fix moved the problem?

Now look right: soft engineering, working with nature. Beach nourishment means adding sand to a beach. In the Netherlands, engineers built the Sand Motor, a giant sandy hook that waves spread along the coast. In Vietnam and Bangladesh, people plant mangrove trees whose roots calm the waves. Which would you choose?

Most places now mix both, and sometimes they choose managed retreat, which means letting the sea take some land and moving back. Great thinking! Challenge: if your town were by the sea, which method would you pick, and why?

faq.a: Hard engineering means building strong structures, like sea walls, rock armour and groynes, to stop the sea. It works well in one place but is expensive and can push the problem further along the coast.
asks: What is the difference between hard and soft engineering?

faq.a: Soft engineering works with nature: adding sand to beaches, planting dunes and mangroves, or letting some land flood. It is cheaper and looks natural, but often has to be repeated.
Groynes are wooden or rock barriers built out into the sea across a beach. They trap sand moving along the coast, but beaches further along then get less sand.
asks: Why do beaches have wooden fences?

faq.a: Mangrove trees grow in salty water, and their tangled roots slow down waves and storm surges and hold the mud in place. The Sundarbans helps shield coasts in Bangladesh and India.
Managed retreat means deciding to let the sea flood or wear away some land on purpose, and moving people and buildings back. The flooded land often becomes salt marsh, which soaks up wave energy.
asks: Why let the sea take land?

facts: The Holderness coast in England erodes by about 1.8 m a year on average, one of the fastest rates in Europe.
The Dutch Sand Motor, built in 2011, placed about 21 million cubic metres of sand off the coast near The Hague.

quiz.say: Which is an example of soft engineering?
quiz.show: An example of soft engineering is…
quiz.why: Mangroves work with nature to calm waves, so they are soft engineering.

wrong.1: A concrete sea wall is hard engineering.

quiz.say: Groynes trap sand on one beach. What can happen further along the coast?
quiz.show: Further along the coast from groynes…

options.show: Beaches lose sand and erode faster
options.say: Beaches lose sand and erode faster

quiz.why: Less sand reaches beaches further along, so they get thinner and the cliffs behind them erode faster.

wrong.1: Groynes cannot stop the waves and tides.
wrong.2: Cliffs never grow taller; they only wear back.
